newsitem.title: UK: No aggressive UK tightening until stg eases-IFS.
newsitem.headline: No aggressive UK tightening until stg eases-IFS.

text.p: The Bank of England, newly empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, is unlikely to start tightening monetary policy aggressively until sterling eases, the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Goldman Sachs International said.

In their "Green Budget," in which they provide analysis and advice on the forthcoming budget, they said the Bank was likely to raise rates gradually from the present 6.25 percent until there were clear signs that growth was slowing and inflation pressures were abating.

"On occasion, the Bank of England has played down the importance of sterling, but there is little doubt that the exchange rate is taken into account when the Bank considers interest rates, not least because it has a significant impact on the short-term inflation outlook," they said.
"Thus, despite its newly gained independence, the Bank of England is unlikely to start tightening monetary policy aggressively until the sterling exchange rate softens."
The Green Budget said that at existing exchange rates, the current account could move from balance last year to a deficit of over two percent of GDP in 1998.

"At some point, the worsening current account deficit will undermine the exchange rate; interest rates might then need to be raised sharply to prevent a market pickup in inflation -- in effect, a mini re-run of 1998."
This potential conflict could be avoided if sterling were to depreciate, but this might be beyond the control of the authorities in the near term, the report added.
The value of the pound in the coming months could be determined as much by events outside the UK as by domestic factors.
For example, a marked deterioration in the trade balance could undermine sterling, as could a more aggressive tightening in monetary policy in the U.S. than in Britain.
In the longer term, the IFS and Goldman said the policy dilemmas caused by the strong pound could dissipate of their own accord.
According to Goldman Sachs estimates, sterling and the dollar had both become overvalued.
"Both currencies are forecast to weaken over the next year against other currencies as their relative growth advantage diminishes and their respective balance of payments worsen," the report said.
